newsitem.title: USA: Greenpeace protests soybeans that Monsanto defends.
newsitem.headline: Greenpeace protests soybeans that Monsanto defends.

text.p: Five Greenpeace protesters were arrested for disrupting cargo loadings at a grain terminal in a protest over genetically altered soybeans, authorities said on Wednesday.

Greenpeace is protesting over exports of genetically altered soybeans developed by Monsanto Co. to withstand its "Roundup" herbicide. Farmers who plant the altered crops can spray fields with the herbicide without harming the crop.
The environmental group says the altered soybeans were not tested adequately by the St. Louis-based firm before approval for human consumption. It wants them segregated from other soybeans.
Monsanto, facing protests from Greenpeace in the United States and Europe, defended scientific tests that it said back up its safety claims.
"We did something like 1,800 tests to evaluate those soybeans," Karen Marshall, manager of public affairs for Monsanto, said. "These soybeans are absolutely safe."

A Greenpeace spokeswoman said about 25 activists protested at a loading terminal here operated by Cargill, the world's largest grain trading company. Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc. handles about 350 million bushels of grain and oilseeds at the Reserve terminal each year, according to company officials.

The protesters, some in inflatable boats, plastered bright yellow posters reading "X-Genetic Experiment" on two grain ships on Tuesday before the Coast Guard set up an exclusion zone to move protesters back, Greenpeace spokeswoman Tzporah Berman said.
Five people were arrested and charged with criminal trespass, police said. Bond for each was set at $5,000.

"Our operations at Reserve, Louisiana, were only shut down for one hour on Nov. 19," Cargill spokeswoman Lori Johnson said. "It was basically a minor disruption and we chose to stop loading for that brief period for safety reasons so that the Greenpeace folks would not be injured."
Greenpeace activists in Frankfurt, Germany, on Wednesday also protested the European Union's decision to approve imports of products made from genetically altered soybeans.

Greenpeace has raised concerns about residues of the herbicide. "As such the tests provide no information about the residue of this poison in the plants," Greenpeace's German campaign leader Joerg Naumann told a news conference.

Monsanto's Marshall, however, said Roundup residue was not an issue since tolerance levels for the herbicide had been previously established and did not need more testing. Monsanto's tests focused on genetic alteration.
"What we figured would be the new piece of information was the one protein that we added to the plant itself," she said.

Marshall said Roundup Ready soybeans had been approved by regulatory bodies in Argentina, Mexico, Canada Japan, the EU and the United States. She said they had also received food safety approvals in Britain, the Netherlands and Denmark.

Last week 17 Greepeace protesters were arrested at the Archer Daniels Midland grain terminal in Destrehan, Louisiana, after nine chained themselves to the facility's gate and eight others chained themselves inside two grain barges.
Greenpeace also blockaded shipments of soybeans imported by Cargill in Antwerp and Ghent, Belgium last week.
